title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:1–25)
hook: the king on a donkey, a withered tree, and pray believing and forgive

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder, threw off his cloak, and followed Jesus on the way. Your line was what wilt thou. Today, that road reaches the gates of Jerusalem.

Palm branches carried into church once a year, in the Palm Sunday procession: it starts here. Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey, a colt nobody has ever ridden, and rides it down into Jerusalem. People throw their cloaks on the road, cut down branches, and shout. It looks like a king arriving. Then, over the next day, he does two very strange things. He curses a fig tree. And he turns over tables in the Temple. Mark weaves the two together.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY STARTS HERE.` → `A KING ON A YOUNG DONKEY.` → `A FIG TREE, AND THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: First, the shout. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna, blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna is a cry from the psalms, a plea to the Lord to save, and Catholics still sing or say it at Mass, in the Holy, Holy, before the consecration. A king, but on a donkey, not a war horse. Second, the fig tree. Next morning he's hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing but leaves. Mark adds, strangely, that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus says no one will eat fruit from it again. Third, the Temple. He walks into the Temple courts, drives out the sellers, overturns the money changers' tables, and says: "My house shall be called the house of prayer to all nations? But you have made it a den of thieves." He's quoting two prophets, Isaiah and Jeremiah. The next morning the fig tree is withered from the roots. It's a Mark sandwich: tree, Temple, tree. Some readers hear the tree as a sign, the way prophets acted out signs: all leaves, no fruit, wrapped around the scene at the Temple. Fourth, what Jesus says about it all: not a lesson in cursing, a lesson in prayer. Have faith in God; whatever you ask in prayer, believe. Then the line that ends today's reading: "when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man; that your Father also, who is in heaven, may forgive you your sins." In Mark's order, forgiving comes before asking.
screen: `HOSANNA: A CRY TO BE SAVED.` · `LEAVES, AND NO FRUIT.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `WHEN YOU STAND TO PRAY, FORGIVE.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Let one face come to mind, someone you're holding something against; not the biggest wound you have, start smaller, and notice what your body does. Then, if you can, loosen your grip a little: forgiving doesn't mean saying it was fine, it means not carrying it into this moment. If you pray, bring whatever you were going to ask; if you don't, let the space it left be quiet.
Hosanna. The cry from the psalms the crowd shouts as Jesus rides into Jerusalem: a plea to the Lord to save, still sung at Mass. Today's word.
Your line: forgive, then pray. In Mark's order, forgiving comes first. Day two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics reenact the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday with blessed palms and a procession, sing Hosanna in the Sanctus at every Mass, and exchange a sign of peace before Communion as a gesture of reconciliation.

The fig tree reading is kept as a prophetic sign about fruitless worship, framed as what 'many readers hear'; care taken not to present it as a sign against the Jewish people. Keeper should confirm tone.
Hosanna from Hebrew hoshia na, Psalm 118:25 (Vulgate 117:25): confirm the note.
Palm Sunday procession, Sanctus and sign of peace in howItsDone: general practice; confirm.
Outline practice 'forgive before you pray' kept.
